extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of classical literature, philosophy, and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Close critical commentary on Plato's Republic (primarily Books III–IV), extracting principles for art, education, character-selection, and political design. Useful for literary analysts, philosophers, and educators studying Platonic norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style conforms to subject; metre to style
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The style is to conform to the subject and the metre to the style.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proportion between subject, style, and metre must be maintained: metre follows the needs of style, which in turn must suit the subject. This general principle ties poetic form directly to content and underlies judgments about appropriateness in poetry and music.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and harmony as guiding aesthetic principle
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The simplicity and harmony of the soul should be reflected in them all.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity is a central artistic rule to be learned in youth and can be observed in creative/constructive arts and natural forms. Simplicity produces clarity and moral harmony; its absence corrupts taste and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artists must avoid meanness or unseemliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Other artists as well as poets should be warned against meanness or unseemliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sculpture, painting, and music must conform to the law of simplicity; creators who violate this should be excluded because their work corrupts citizens’ tastes and morals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music educates and shapes the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Of all these influences the greatest is the education given by music, which finds a way into the innermost soul and imparts to it the sense of beauty and of deformity.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Music’s effect is first unconscious and later received by reason; it forms perception of beauty/deformity and reduces need for later corrective measures. Thus musical training is essential and must be carefully chosen (simple, characteristic melodies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogy: teach elements first, then combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: As in learning to read, first we acquire the elements or letters separately, and afterwards their combinations... in like manner we must first attain the elements or essential forms of the virtues, and then trace their combinations in life and experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational sequence: isolate basic elements (letters, simple musical forms, elemental virtues), ensure mastery, then move to combinations and complex applications. One cannot recognize composite forms without knowing elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: True art is simple, ideal, not merely imitative
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘True art is not fanciful and imitative, but simple and ideal,—the expression of the highest moral energy, whether in action or repose.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art should express moral energy and ideals rather than mere imitation or fanciful ornament. This conception extends beyond music/plastic arts to pervade nature and all formative educational influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: The work of art should be a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘A work of art, like the State, is a whole.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artistic works should be conceived and judged as integrated wholes rather than as accumulations of parts; unity and proportion are essential criteria in evaluating artworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion between thought and expression; avoid obscurity
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be proportion between style and subject; the thought must not exceed the power of lucid expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid half-expressed figures, harsh constructions, distorted word collocations, and remote sequences. Clarity of language should increase with each generation — do not emulate necessary obscurities of earlier ages (e.g., some early Greek poets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors/poets are poor judges of their own meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The poet has been a bad judge of his own meaning... the word which is full of associations to his own mind is difficult and unmeaning to that of another.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and critics must correct poets’ opaque expressions: what feels charged or clear to the creator can be obscure to readers. Revisions should aim for clearer transfer of associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physician should have experienced illness; judge should be uncorrupted and mature
rubrics_metrics.description: The physician should have had experience of disease in his own body... the judge controls mind by mind; and therefore his mind should not be corrupted by crime... the judge should be of a certain age; his youth should have been innocent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different public roles require different experiential profiles: medical practitioners benefit from personal experience of sickness; judges must be morally untainted and cultivated by observation rather than practice of vice; age and prior innocence are recommended for judicial office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance music and gymnastic to harmonize reason and passion
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two principles in man, reason and passion, and to these... the two arts of music and gymnastic correspond. He who mingles them in harmonious concord is the true musician.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational programs must balance musical (taming, refining) and gymnastic (arousing, sustaining) training. Too much gymnastic hardens and brutalizes; too much music enervates. A measured mixture produces harmony of faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gymnastic and diet for guardians should be simple and austere
rubrics_metrics.description: Our warrior athletes must be wide-awake... they will require a simpler kind of gymnastic, akin to their simple music; and for their diet a rule may be found in Homer... roast meat only... no sweet sauces... Sicilian cookery and Attic confections and Corinthian courtezans... must be forbidden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical training and diet for guardians should cultivate robustness and responsiveness: avoid luxuries, exotic cooking, and indulgences that produce gluttony or softness. Guardians should be inured to changing conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical practice policy: avoid fostering invalidism; 'kill or cure' approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Asclepius would not practise this art, because he knew that the citizens of a well-ordered State have no leisure to be ill... ‘They must be at their business... if they recover, well; if they don’t, there is an end of them.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Medical practice in the ideal state should not nurture chronic invalidism or over-care for intemperate individuals. Treatments that prolong useless lives or encourage weakness are to be avoided; medicine serves the public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and testing of rulers (guardians)
rubrics_metrics.description: These we must select; but they must be watched at every epoch of life to see whether they have retained the same opinions and held out against force and enchantment... tried by many tests, like gold in the refiner’s fire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulers must be selected for disinterested love of subjects and proven by recurring tests (danger, pleasure, grief) across life stages; retention of principles and self-command are key criteria for continued office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of myth (a 'magnificent lie') for civic education
rubrics_metrics.description: We will inform them that their youth was a dream... and that these brothers and sisters have different natures, and some of them God framed to rule... of gold, silver, brass and iron... the tale must be imparted... first to the rulers, then to the soldiers, lastly to the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy a offered myth/noble lie to create social cohesion and inculcate duties and rank. Mythology is pedagogically useful: it simplifies complex moral-political ideas and permits light treatment of controversial principles while persuading citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional rule: guardians must have no private property or gold
rubrics_metrics.description: They should have no property; their pay should only meet their expenses; and they should have common meals... They only of the citizens may not touch it [gold], or be under the same roof with it, or drink from it...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prevent corruption and the descent into householders/tyrants, guardians must be economically restricted (no private land, houses, or wealth) and have communal lifestyles. Economic separation from wealth preserves civic character.

rubrics_metrics.name: State size constrained by unity; education is primary
rubrics_metrics.description: To the size of the state there is no limit but the necessity of unity; it must be neither too large nor too small to be one... all these things are secondary, if education, which is the great matter, be duly regarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political organization should aim for a scope that preserves unity; education is the decisive factor for state health and cohesion rather than fine-grained legislative detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve cultural forms (music/gymnastic) from innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: The care of the governors should be directed to preserve music and gymnastic from innovation; alter the songs of a country, Damon says, and you will soon end by altering its laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural changes, beginning innocently, can erode character and institutions. Guardians should guard traditional cultural forms to maintain moral and legal stability; unnecessary innovation is risky.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic middle condition is best for artisans and citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: A middle condition is best for artisans; they should have money enough to buy tools, and not enough to be independent of business... will not the same condition be best for our citizens?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid extremes of poverty and wealth among citizens: moderate means encourage industry without creating luxury or servility; this balance supports civic virtue and military capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical foundation: priority of duty/right over happiness/utilitarianism
rubrics_metrics.description: First duty, then happiness, is the natural order of our moral ideas... The utilitarian principle is valuable as a corrective of error... But utility is not the historical basis of morality; nor the aspect in which moral and religious ideas commonly occur to the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral and political systems should be grounded in right/truth rather than solely in the maximization of happiness; utilitarian considerations are secondary and instrumental in many contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plato's stylistic devices to note in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Lesser matters of style: (1) The affected ignorance of music (2) The tentative manner (3) The description of the State sometimes as a reality, and then again as a work of imagination (4) Connecting links for expulsion of poets (5) Companion pictures and satirical jests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing Plato’s style, mark rhetorical effects—irony, tentativeness, shifts between fiction and reality, connective strategies, and satire. These devices shape persuasion and should be considered when evaluating argument and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of exaggeration in Plato's claims about music and mind–body control
rubrics_metrics.description: Two paradoxes: (1) the great power of music, so much beyond modern experience; (2) the almost absolute control which the soul is supposed to exercise over the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should treat Plato’s emphatic claims with caution: there is likely some exaggeration and Pythagorean numerological influence. Distinguish genuine insight from hyperbolic rhetoric, and note confusions (e.g., musical harmony vs. harmony of soul).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition of ranks and conditional meritocracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato’s transposition of ranks: some are fashioned to rule, others to be auxiliaries, others husbandmen and craftsmen... but a golden parent may have a silver son, and then there must be a change of rank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political systems should recognize both inherited distinctions and the need for periodic mobility on grounds of merit. Plato proposes tests and occasional breaches of fixed caste to allow talent to rise, taught via mythological narrative rather than detailed procedure.
